Footnote 11 reports null effects of classroom quality on turnover, attached to a Discussion sentence asserting that misclassification 'could unintentionally exacerbate turnover in precisely the schools most in need.' Footnotes 5 and 6 hold the roster-linking limitation and the sample restrictions that drop 17%, 15%, and 21% of rosters at successive stages — exclusions the main text never quantifies.
- Terminology invites misreading. 'Classroom quality index' names a composite of students' incoming test scores, GPA, attendance, suspensions, and grade repetition — it measures who is in the room, not the quality of instruction in it. The definition is clear on first use, but the shorthand then runs through every table row label, every heterogeneity discussion, and the title's word 'composition,' which most education-research readers will read as demographics — precisely the dimension the paper reports as null for observation scores.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Do not quote the introduction's '0.13 SD increase in student survey scores.' The survey effect in the preferred specification is 0.152 (0.042) — Table 2, Column 10, narrated correctly in the results as 0.15 SD. The 0.13 is the observation-score effect estimated on the survey sample (Supplemental Appendix Table A9). Quote 0.07 SD for observations (Table 2, Column 4 = 0.068) and 0.15 SD for surveys (Column 10).
- Read Table 2 in two vertical strips and anchor on Columns 4 and 10 — everything else is a build-up. Note that Columns 5/11 (quality only) and 6/12 (demographics only) omit the rows they exclude, so the classroom-quality row carries 10 values across 12 columns; count carefully before aligning a coefficient with a column. Columns 4 and 10 are the paper.
- For the survey results, read Columns 7 through 10 across, not just Column 10. Share Black runs +0.414*** → +0.407*** → −0.512* → −0.921** as fixed effects are added, and share FRPL is positive throughout (0.578 to 0.928). The prose reports only the final column and never flags the sign reversal or the positive FRPL association. Treat these as between-school versus within-teacher comparisons telling opposite stories, and do not cite the abstract's 'no consistent association' for surveys.
- Spend real time on Table 5 rather than the paragraph summarizing it. Panel A, Column 5 (t+1) is 0.033** — significant at p < .05, not 'marginally significant' as the text says, and about half the contemporaneous 0.068. Panel B's t−1 (0.079) and t−2 (0.091) are insignificant but not small relative to the 0.152 concurrent effect. The exogeneity case is defensible but weaker than the prose asserts; form your own judgment from the coefficients.
- In Table 6, look at Column 5 — the one the text skips. Value-added is +0.131*** without teacher-by-school fixed effects and −0.148*** with them (Column 6). The mechanism argument rests entirely on the FE estimate, and the paper itself concedes that the negative sign may reflect higher-baseline students having 'less room to grow.' Read 'points instead toward evaluator bias as the primary mechanism' as the authors' interpretation of suggestive evidence, not a demonstrated finding; the two supporting tests are a null interaction and a growth coefficient with an admitted mechanical explanation.
- Read footnote 10 before reading the Policy Simulations section — it is the single most consequential sentence outside the main text. Black teachers' classroom-quality gap is 0.9 SD across schools but about 0.06 SD within schools, so the simulated 8.3-percentile gain is driven by cross-school sorting while the adjustment coefficient is identified from much smaller within-teacher-school variation. Read footnote 11 alongside the Discussion's turnover paragraph: the footnote reports null turnover effects the paragraph's speculation does not mention. Footnotes 5 and 6 (roster linking; the 17%/15%/21% sample exclusions) belong to the same must-read set.
- Verify any number before quoting it. Three text–table mismatches are confirmed: the middle-school coefficient is 0.106, not the '0.125 SD' in the text (Table 3, Column 10); the abstract's '8 percentage points' should be 8 percentile points (Table 7, Column 7 = 8.29); and the R2 'from .20 to .80' corresponds to no pair in Table 2 (.16/.24/.41 → .84). Also note the survey sample is described as 3,345 unique teachers in the text but 4,066 in every regression table, and the Table 1 note's year range (2011–12 onward) disagrees with the Data section's 2012–13 to 2016–17.
- Substitute 'classroom composition on incoming student achievement and behavior' whenever you see 'classroom quality.' The index is baseline test scores, GPA, attendance, suspensions, and grade repetition — student inputs, not instructional quality. The title's 'composition' likewise does not mean demographics, which the paper reports as null for observation scores.
- A time-constrained reader can skim the Related Literature section, the CPS institutional description, and the Heterogeneity section (Table 3 is a uniformity check that finds little), and can skip the Properties of Regression-Adjusted Scores paragraph. Do not skip: the Conceptual Framework's Assumption 1, Table 2 Columns 4 and 10, Table 5, Table 6, Table 7 Columns 7–9, footnotes 5/6/10/11, and the Discussion's over-correction paragraph — the last is the paper's own strongest caveat and is absent from the abstract, whose final sentence and the conclusion's closing paragraph both read as unqualified advocacy.
- If you only have the article and not the Supplemental Appendix, be aware that several claims the text emphasizes are unverifiable: the domain-level results (Tables A8, A10), the survey-sample observation replication that produced the disputed 0.13 (Table A9), the full-covariate-vector specifications (Table A7), and the survey policy simulation (Table A13). The observation-score claims can be checked in-article; the domain and survey-sample claims cannot.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Column reconstruction and verification method. Table 2's 12 columns were reconstructed by matching row-value counts to the specification structure: the classroom-quality row carries 10 values (Columns 6 and 12 are demographics-only) and each demographic row also carries 10 (Columns 5 and 11 are quality-only), giving the mapping 1,2,3,4,6 / 7,8,9,10,12 for demographics and 1,2,3,4,5 / 7,8,9,10,11 for the index. Three independent cross-checks confirm the mapping: Column 4's 0.068 reappears as Table 3 Panel A Column 1, as Table 5 Panel A Column 4, and as Table 6 Column 1; Column 10's 0.152 reappears as Table 3 Panel B Column 1 and Table 5 Panel B Column 4. Every number cited above was read from the article; equations, Greek symbols, the Table A5 correlations, and the 0.31/0.82 variance ratio were treated as extraction artifacts and are not assessed.

What came out clean. Several plausible-sounding problems are not problems, and readers should not chase them. The 'Exit top 5%' sign reading is correct: the outcome is defined as moving below the 95th percentile after adjustment, so Table 7 Column 9's Black coefficient of −0.16*** does mean a higher likelihood of remaining in the top 5%, exactly as the text says. The Table 2 N(teachers) difference of 4,067 versus 4,066 is not an inconsistency: Columns 6 and 12 use the full samples (30,479 and 10,991) while Columns 1–5 and 7–11 drop the observations missing the classroom quality index (29,078 and 10,990), matching Table 1's reported index observation counts exactly; one survey observation and one teacher are lost. The Table 4 narration is accurate throughout (0.053 and 0.064 for 'about 0.05–0.06 SD'; stability at 0.053/0.058 in Columns 2 and 5; the marginally significant 0.032* interaction; the null survey interactions of 0.007 and −0.020). Table 6's column citations are correct — Column 3 is the performance-task estimate with fixed effects (−1.037**) and Column 6 the value-added estimate with fixed effects (−0.148***). Table 7's tournament figures (7.16, 2.13, 0.50, −0.70, 0.07) all match. The 'R2 0.68' versus '.68' formatting in Table 2's last column and the leading-zero inconsistency between Tables 5/6 are cosmetic and affect nothing.

Why the rating is 'adequate' rather than 'strong.' The exposition itself is good: the argument is built in a logical order, each empirical section announces what threat it is addressing, the tables are self-documenting, and the paper resists most of the temptations to overclaim (the Discussion's over-correction paragraph is a genuine concession, and the survey section volunteers the demographic results the abstract omits). Against that, six distinct numerical or labeling errors survived two revision rounds and production, and they are not randomly distributed — each one runs in the direction that makes the paper look tidier: the introduction's survey effect is a different estimate entirely, the middle-school coefficient is inflated by 18%, a p < .05 placebo lead is downgraded to 'marginal,' an interaction the paper elsewhere calls marginally significant becomes 'indistinguishable from zero' when it is used to support the evaluator-bias mechanism, the abstract's demographics null holds for only one of two outcomes, and the abstract's units convert percentile points into percentage points. None of these overturns a headline result — the observation effect of 0.068 and the survey effect of 0.152 are what the tables say, the placebo pattern is broadly supportive, and the equity simulation is correctly reported in the body. But the cumulative effect is that the prose cannot be used as a substitute for the exhibits. A reader quoting this paper should quote the tables.

Abstract fidelity specifically. The abstract does not report the 0.07/0.13 pair — that is the introduction — so the abstract's factual content is thinner than the introduction's and correspondingly harder to falsify. Its three assertions are: (1) higher-achieving, less disruptive classrooms yield higher ratings — supported; (2) effects are robust across specifications, placebo tests, and dimensions of practice — mostly supported, though 'placebo tests' glosses the significant t+1 lead; (3) demographics show no consistent association — true for observations, false for surveys in the paper's own preferred column. Its policy sentence has the units wrong. What the abstract omits matters as much: no mention of the evaluator-bias mechanism claim that the body treats as a central finding, and no trace of the Discussion's warning that mechanical adjustment 'could over-correct, masking true variation in teaching effectiveness.' The abstract is not misleading about the paper's direction, but it is systematically smoother than the paper.

Navigability and where the argument actually lives. The structure is standard and works well. The load-bearing exhibits are few: Table 2 Columns 4 and 10 (the two headline effects), Table 5 (whether the design is credible), Table 6 (the mechanism), and Table 7 Columns 7–9 (the equity payoff). Everything else is supporting. The real navigability problem is vertical rather than horizontal: the paper's four most consequential qualifications — cross-school versus within-school variation in classroom assignment (fn. 10), null turnover effects (fn. 11), the roster-linking and multi-section measurement-error limitation (fn. 5), and the scale of the sample exclusions (fn. 6) — are all in footnotes, and a substantial share of the results the text discusses at length (domain-level effects, the survey-sample replication, the full-covariate specifications, the survey policy simulation) exist only in a Supplemental Appendix that does not travel with the article. A reader working from the PDF alone has the main results but cannot audit the intermediate steps, including the one that produced the introduction's mis-attributed 0.13.

---

### Contribution Review

**Rating:** Strong (moderate confidence)

Delgado and Sartain move the classroom-composition-and-observation-ratings question out of the MET video lab and into an actual high-stakes district evaluation system, showing with teacher-by-school fixed effects that the same teacher in the same school earns 0.068 SD higher principal observation ratings and 0.152 SD higher student survey ratings per 1 SD of a classroom academic/behavioral quality index. The direction of the finding confirms Steinberg and Garrett (2016) and Campbell and Ronfeldt (2018) rather than overturning them; the genuine contributions are the authentic-stakes, all-subjects, district-scale setting, the parallel high-stakes/low-stakes comparison, and a first-of-its-kind equity simulation of adjusting observation scores. Its two most quotable claims — that the mechanism is evaluator bias, and that adjustment raises Black teachers' rankings by 8 percentile points — rest on considerably weaker evidence than its core estimates do.

**Strengths:**

- Setting is the real contribution: authentic REACH ratings (70% of a teacher's evaluation, with remediation and dismissal consequences) assigned in person by principals to the near-universe of CPS grades 3–8 teachers across all subjects — 30,479 teacher-years, 10,934 teachers. Prior causal evidence came from trained external raters scoring videotaped lessons for small volunteer samples. This is the setting policymakers actually govern, and the paper is now the best available evidence there.
- The design does real work rather than decorating an existing correlation. The raw association is 0.172 SD (Table 2, Col. 1), 0.094 SD with school fixed effects (Col. 3), and 0.068 SD within teacher-by-school (Col. 4). Reporting that ladder honestly tells readers that roughly 60% of the headline correlation in this literature is sorting — a quantification that is itself a contribution and one that cuts against the paper's own framing.
- The exogeneity case is unusually well-built for a fixed-effects paper: lead/lag placebo tests (Table 5) are null at t−3 through t−1 and t+2/t+3 (only t+1 = 0.033 is significant, and the authors flag it as likely multiple-testing noise), a correlated-shocks test on demographic composition, robustness to experienced teachers only, small classes, elementary self-contained classrooms, and controls for prior-year observation score and value-added.
- The high-stakes/low-stakes comparison is genuinely novel. Students — who face no incentive, and whose ratings are excluded from evaluation — respond about as strongly (0.152 SD) as principals do on the same middle-grade subsample (~0.13 SD). That parallelism is the most interesting under-discussed result in the paper: whatever is going on is not specific to raters with stakes.
- The policy simulation is new to this literature and is reported with appropriate technical care: adjusted and unadjusted observation scores correlate at 0.91, year-to-year reliability falls only from 0.75 to 0.69, and the rank–rank correlation with district VAM moves from 0.23 to 0.21. Readers can see that the adjustment does not destroy the measure's other properties.
- The paper is candid where it counts. Footnote 10 discloses that most classroom-quality variation is between schools (Black teachers are assigned classrooms 0.9 SD lower across schools but only ~0.06 SD lower within them); footnote 11 reports null effects on school exit; the Discussion explicitly warns that mechanical adjustment could over-correct if sorting reflects genuine quality differences.

**Weaknesses:**

- The evaluator-bias conclusion is the paper's most-quoted claim and its least-supported one. Table 6 shows classroom quality lowers performance-task scores (−1.037) and value-added (−0.148) under teacher-by-school fixed effects — but the authors themselves supply the confound in the same paragraph: higher-baseline students have less room to grow. Growth measures are mechanically negatively related to baseline achievement, so a genuine positive performance effect would still show up as a negative coefficient. The test cannot distinguish 'no genuine effect' from 'genuine positive effect masked by mean reversion,' which makes 'points instead toward evaluator bias' an inference the design does not license. The second mechanism test — null interactions with baseline teacher quality (Table 4) — is stated in the paper itself as consistent with either bias or a uniform interaction effect.
- 'Classroom demographics show no consistent association' (abstract) is too clean for the paper's own results. In the survey sample, a 10 pp higher Black share predicts 0.09 SD lower survey scores (Table 2, Col. 10: −0.921), and even in observations the domain-level breakdowns show Black share lowering Classroom Environment (−0.03 SD per 10 pp) and Instruction (−0.02 SD). The demographic nulls also rest on very thin identifying variation — the text reports that only 0.8% of variation in Black share is within-teacher — so 'no effect' here is closer to 'no power' than to a precise zero, and the wide standard error on Black share in Col. 4 (−0.217, SE 0.133) is consistent with that.
- The 8-percentile-point equity headline does not come from the causal design. Equation 6 strips out teacher characteristics and teacher-by-school fixed effects; the adjustment is a cross-sectional residualization on the full 0.172-style gradient, and by footnote 10 the composition differences it corrects are overwhelmingly cross-school. So the simulation corrects for exactly the sorting the identification strategy was built to hold constant. Readers taking '8 points' as the magnitude of within-teacher evaluator bias against Black teachers will be off by a large factor.
- The realized magnitude is modest and easy to overstate. Within-teacher SD of the classroom quality index is 0.31 against a total SD of 0.82, so a typical year-to-year shock is roughly 0.4 index SDs and moves observation scores by something on the order of 0.03 SD. 'Systematically higher' is accurate as a statement about a coefficient; it is not the same as saying real teachers routinely swing meaningfully in ratings because their roster changed. Footnote 11's null turnover results point the same way: composition moves scores but not the consequential outcome tested.
- The measurement structure is coarser than the claims. Rosters pool all of a teacher's sections because the data do not record which classroom was observed; the sample matches students to teachers via whoever assigned the final grade (footnote 5); and there are no rater identifiers, so 'evaluator bias' can never be tested at the level of the evaluator. Restrictions are substantial (17% of rosters dropped for fewer than five students with lagged scores, 15% for >25% special education, 21% for >200 students), and the survey sample is a distinctly different population — 36% match rate, middle-grade English/math/science only.
- The middle-school/elementary split (0.106 vs. 0.054) is treated as a passing note, but it is a factor-of-two difference in the central estimate and shares a boundary with the survey sample. Readers should not treat 0.068 as a portable parameter across grade levels.
- One small consistency issue worth knowing when quoting the paper: the text describes R² rising 'from .20 to .80' when teacher-by-school fixed effects are added, while Table 2 reports .41 → .84. Cite the table.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- CITE IT FOR: the existence and approximate size of a causal within-teacher composition effect on authentic, high-stakes principal observation ratings in a large urban district — 0.068 SD per 1 SD of a baseline achievement/behavior index (Table 2, Col. 4). This is now the best available evidence on that specific question and the natural successor citation to the MET studies for anyone writing about real evaluation systems rather than research settings.
- CITE IT FOR: the decomposition of the well-known raw gradient. The 0.172 → 0.094 → 0.068 ladder is the paper's most defensible quantitative service to the field: most of the observed correlation between classroom disadvantage and low ratings reflects sorting, not rating distortion, but a real causal remainder survives.
- CITE IT FOR: the finding that low-stakes student surveys are at least as composition-sensitive as high-stakes principal ratings (0.152 SD vs. ~0.13 SD on the same subsample). This is the paper's most novel empirical fact and undercuts a common assumption that student surveys are a cleaner alternative to administrator observation.
- CITE IT FOR: prior achievement and attendance — not demographics — as the operative dimension of classroom composition in observation scores, once teacher-by-school fixed effects absorb sorting.
- CITE IT FOR: the technical feasibility of a VAM-style adjustment to observation scores without wrecking the measure (0.91 correlation with unadjusted, reliability 0.75 → 0.69, rank–rank with VAM 0.23 → 0.21). That is a real result about the adjustment's properties, independent of whether the adjustment is normatively right.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: 'evaluator bias is the mechanism.' Table 6's growth measures are mechanically negatively related to baseline achievement, so the test cannot separate bias from a genuine performance channel — the authors' own Discussion concedes that the two are not distinguished, and the paper's abstract and mechanism section run ahead of that.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: 'observation ratings are not biased by student race.' The demographic nulls rest on almost no within-teacher variation (0.8% for Black share), and the survey and domain-level results show significant negative Black-share associations. Read this as unresolved, not as a null.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: '8 percentile points' as the magnitude of within-teacher bias against Black teachers. It comes from a cross-sectional adjustment that corrects the between-school sorting the causal design deliberately holds fixed (footnote 10: 0.9 SD across schools vs. 0.06 SD within). Cite it as 'what a district-wide adjustment policy would do to rankings,' which is what it actually simulates.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: an endorsement of adjusting observation scores. The paper's own Discussion warns that if effective teachers sort into higher-achieving classrooms, mechanical adjustment over-corrects and masks true variation — and the simulation's gains flow through exactly that sorting channel. Anyone citing this to support a policy recommendation should cite the caveat in the same breath.
- DO NOT LEAN ON IT FOR: consequences. Footnote 11 reports null effects of classroom quality on school exit, including for untenured teachers and those with prior low ratings. The paper documents a measurement distortion; it does not document that the distortion changes careers.
- BOUNDARIES: one district (CPS), one rubric (a Danielson adaptation), principal and assistant-principal raters, 2012–13 to 2016–17, grades 3–8, pooled rosters rather than observed sections, surveys only for grades 6–8 English/math/science. The elementary/middle gap (0.054 vs. 0.106) means the pooled 0.068 should not be transported to a specific grade band without noting it.
- OPEN QUESTIONS THIS SETS UP: rater-identified data to test whether the same evaluator rates the same teacher differently as the roster changes (the direct bias test this paper cannot run); section-level rosters linked to the specific observed lesson; replication in districts with different rubrics, external raters, or peer observers; teacher–student race match interacted with composition, which the CPS data could support; whether the rubric itself (footnote 9's cultural-bias concern) rather than the rater is the locus; and — the question this paper's own Discussion raises but leaves open — how to adjust ratings without over-correcting away genuine differences in performance across settings.

**Detailed Commentary:**

Novelty. The finding that teachers of higher-achieving students get higher observation ratings is not new, and the paper does not claim it is. Steinberg and Garrett (2016) and Campbell and Ronfeldt (2018) already established it causally using MET's within-school random assignment. What Delgado and Sartain add is the transplant: from trained external raters scoring videos for a volunteer sample of tested-subject teachers, to principals conducting in-person, career-consequential observations of essentially all grades 3–8 teachers in the country's then-third-largest district, across arts, music, and other untested subjects. That is a substantial external-validity upgrade on the single most-used measure in American teacher evaluation, and the field should treat this as the reference citation for the authentic-stakes setting.

Three further elements are new rather than confirmatory. First, the high-stakes/low-stakes contrast: students rating the same teachers on a survey excluded from evaluation show a larger composition sensitivity (0.152 SD) than principals do, and about the same as principals on the matched middle-grade subsample. Second, the equity simulation, which as far as this literature goes is the first attempt to quantify who wins and loses under a composition adjustment to observation scores. Third, the quantitative decomposition of the raw gradient — 0.172 unadjusted, 0.094 with school FE, 0.068 within teacher-school — which tells the field that the striking descriptive pattern everyone cites (Whitehurst et al.'s near-fourfold gap; this paper's Figure 1, where 40% of bottom-quartile-classroom teachers land in the bottom rating quartile and 11% in the top) is mostly sorting.

The gap between quotable and supported. This paper will be cited heavily, and there is a real risk of it being cited for the wrong three sentences.

Mechanism. The abstract-level claim propagated through the Discussion is that composition effects reflect evaluator bias rather than genuine performance change, based on Table 6: classroom quality raises observation scores (0.068, 0.083) but lowers performance-task (−1.037) and value-added (−0.148) growth measures under the same fixed effects. The authors call this 'stark opposition' and say it is 'difficult to reconcile with the student–teacher interaction hypothesis.' But they also state the alternative explanation one sentence earlier — higher-baseline students have less room to grow — and then set it aside as not mattering. It matters a great deal. Growth measures are constructed from baseline scores and are known to carry a negative mechanical relationship to them; that is a large part of why VAMs are controversial in the first place. Under such a confound, a null coefficient on growth is not evidence of no genuine performance effect, and a negative one is not evidence against it. The test has no way to place the counterfactual. Note also that the VA coefficient flips sign from +0.131 without teacher fixed effects (Col. 5) to −0.148 with them (Col. 6), which should make a reader cautious about treating the fixed-effects VA specification as a clean productivity yardstick. The second mechanism test — null interactions between classroom quality and prior teacher quality (Table 4, Cols. 3 and 6) — is described by the authors themselves as 'consistent with evaluator bias or with a broadly similar interaction effect across teachers.' Neither test is dispositive, and the paper's own conclusion is more confident than either supports.

Demographics. 'Classroom demographics show no consistent association with performance ratings' is stated in the abstract without qualification. Three things complicate it. Within-teacher variation in Black share is 0.8% of total variation, so the fixed-effects specification is nearly powerless on this margin — the Col. 4 estimate is −0.217 with SE 0.133, which does not exclude economically meaningful effects. In the survey sample, where the effect survives, a 10 pp higher Black share predicts 0.09 SD lower survey scores. And even in the observation data, the domain-level results show Black share lowering Classroom Environment and Instruction ratings. The paper reports all of this fairly in the body; the abstract does not, and abstracts are what get cited.

The 8 points. Equation 6 deliberately drops teacher characteristics and teacher-by-school fixed effects, residualizing raw ratings on the classroom quality index and year effects. That is the right thing to do if you want to simulate what a district would actually implement, but it means the resulting ranking changes are driven by the full cross-sectional gradient, not the identified within-teacher parameter. Footnote 10 makes explicit that the classroom-composition gap for Black teachers is 0.9 SD across schools and about 0.06 SD within them. So the 8.29-point gain in Table 7, Col. 7 is overwhelmingly a correction for cross-school sorting — for the fact that Black teachers work in schools serving lower-achieving students. Whether that correction is warranted is a normative question about what evaluation should measure; it is emphatically not established by the within-teacher bias estimate. The paper's own Discussion caveat about over-correction is precisely this concern, and it deserves to travel with the number.

Magnitude. 0.068 SD per full SD of the index is real but small, and the realized within-teacher exposure is smaller still: within-teacher SD of the index is 0.31 against a total of 0.82, so a typical roster shock is on the order of 0.4 index SDs and shifts ratings by roughly 0.03 SD. 'Systematically higher' is a defensible description of a precisely estimated coefficient; it should not be read as saying that composition swings routinely reshuffle teachers in the rating distribution. Footnote 11's null turnover findings are the consistency check on this, and they point in the modest direction.

Generalizability. The boundaries are drawn honestly in the text, if not always in the abstract. One district, one rubric, principal raters, 2012–2017, grades 3–8, with surveys confined to middle-grade English/math/science. The pooled-roster construction means classroom characteristics are measured with error relative to the actual observed section; the authors address this with small-class and elementary subsamples and find similar magnitudes (0.05–0.07), which is reassuring. The elementary/middle gap (0.054 vs. 0.106) is the biggest internal heterogeneity and is underplayed. Whether the effect generalizes to districts with external or peer observers, to different rubrics, or to the post-2017 era of generally softened evaluation stakes is untested.

Standing and follow-on work. For the question 'does classroom composition causally shift ratings in a real high-stakes evaluation system,' this is now the best available evidence, and the placebo and correlated-shocks tests make it credible within its identifying assumption. For 'why,' the field is roughly where Campbell and Ronfeldt left it — the paper asserts a mechanism it does not identify. For 'what should districts do,' the paper opens a policy conversation it does not settle, and its own over-correction caveat is the honest bottom line. The most valuable follow-ons it sets up are rater-identified data (the direct evaluator-bias test), section-level rosters matched to the specific observed lesson, replication across rubrics and rater types, teacher–student race match, and the question raised in footnote 9 but never tested — whether the bias resides in the rater or in a rubric that centers particular classroom practices.

---

### Reproducibility Review

**Rating:** Adequate (moderate confidence)

The article is transparent about its models and its estimation samples — Equation 4 is enumerated variable-by-variable, standard-error rules are stated, and every table reports SEs, R-squared, observation counts and teacher counts by column — but it carries no data availability statement, no replication package, no code, and no software statement of any kind, and several load-bearing constructed variables (the PCA classroom quality index, the survey composite, the observation composite, and the district's value-added and performance-task measures) cannot be rebuilt exactly from what is written. A replicator with CPS/Consortium data access could re-run the headline specification and would likely land close, but would have to guess on the index construction, the survey item handling, and the policy-simulation ranking rules, and would hit at least three unexplained numerical inconsistencies in the reported sample counts.

**Strengths:**

- Data sources are named precisely — de-identified CPS administrative files (student demographics, test scores, attendance, transcripts, teacher personnel files, REACH evaluation data) plus the 5Essentials student survey fielded through the UChicago Consortium on School Research — and the Acknowledgments name the specific institutional gatekeepers (Consortium staff, Elaine Allensworth, John Q. Easton, the CPS Talent Office), so a would-be replicator knows exactly whose door to knock on even though no formal access procedure is documented.
- The main specification is genuinely re-runnable from prose. The text spells out the full right-hand side of Equation 4: the classroom quality index, share male, shares Black and non-Black non-Hispanic (Hispanic omitted as the largest group), share FRPL, share special education, log roster size, and the complete teacher covariate list (gender, race/ethnicity indicators, age, experience and experience squared, tenure, no-college-degree indicator, no-teaching-certificate indicator, graduate degree, National Board Certification), with teacher-by-school and year fixed effects.
- Inference conventions are stated explicitly rather than left to guesswork: robust standard errors in specifications with teacher-by-school fixed effects, clustered at the teacher level in specifications without them (stated in the text and repeated in the Table 2 and Table 6 notes), and clustered at the teacher level throughout Table 7. Standardization is stated repeatedly — both the dependent variables and the classroom quality index are standardized by year to mean 0, SD 1.
- Sample restrictions are collected in a dedicated footnote (note 6) with a drop share at each step, and the linking procedure and its limitations are documented candidly rather than buried: notes 4 and 5 explain that rosters are built from transcript files using the teacher who assigned final grades, that all sections are pooled because the data do not record which section was observed, and that this induces measurement error — which is then addressed with the small-class and elementary subsamples in Table 3.
- Several transparency details that most papers omit are present: note 7 documents teacher-covariate missingness (<2%, mean imputation for continuous, zero for indicators, missing-value flags included, experience set to 0 in the first observed year), note 2 documents survey Likert handling, note 3 reports that PC1 explains 40% of joint variation and points to sensitivity checks using later components and the raw vector, and note 10 reports the between- versus within-school decomposition motivating the policy design.
- Every regression table reports N, N (teachers), R-squared, and explicit control-set indicator rows, so the estimation sample for each column is legible; the policy adjustment is formally defined (Equations 6 and 7 — the residual from a regression of the rating on the classroom quality index and year fixed effects), and the Figure 1 note independently restates the same definition, so the adjusted-score construction is unambiguous.

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data availability statement, no replication package, no code repository, no analysis-software or version statement, and no stated data-access pathway anywhere in the article. A full-text search for 'available' (in a data sense), 'replication', 'code', 'Stata', 'R', 'GitHub', 'OSF', 'data-use', 'agreement', 'restricted', 'request', 'deposit', 'archive', 'review board', and 'IRB' returns nothing relevant — not even a boilerplate 'available upon request'. The article names no CPS Research Review Board process and no Consortium data-sharing procedure. Restricted administrative data legitimately preclude posting the data, but for a 2026 AERA journal article the absence of any statement, and of any code, falls below current journal-era norms.
- The sample-construction funnel cannot be reconstructed or audited. Note 6 begins 'Starting with grades 1–8 teachers' while the Sample Description says 'Our sample includes all grades 3–8 teachers'; the three drop shares (rosters with fewer than five lagged-tested students, 17%; rosters over 25% special education, 15%; rosters over 200 students, 21%) are not labeled as sequential or as shares of the original base, and — decisively — the number of teachers or teacher-years in the starting universe is never reported. With 30,479 surviving teacher-years and no denominator, the restrictions cannot be checked in either direction. The Table 1 note further describes only one of the three restrictions ('linked to at least five students with non-missing baseline test scores').
- The panel span is stated two different ways. The Data section says 'de-identified administrative and survey data from CPS for the 2012–2013 to 2016–2017 school years' (five years), while the Table 1 note says the statistics are 'from Chicago Public Schools between the 2011–2012 and 2016–2017 school years' (six years). Compounding this, the institutional section states REACH covered only non-tenured teachers in 2012–2013 and expanded to all teachers in 2013–2014, so whether 2012–2013 is in the observation sample — and therefore whether the first panel year is a selected non-tenured population against which scores are year-standardized — is left unresolved. Teacher-years per year cannot be pinned down (30,479 over five years is ~6,100/year; over four years, ~7,600/year).
- A 1,401-observation gap is never explained. Table 1 reports 30,479 observations for every classroom characteristic except classroom quality, which has 29,078; correspondingly Table 2 columns 1–5 (which include the index) use N = 29,078 with 10,354 teachers, while column 6 (demographics only) uses N = 30,479 with 10,934 teachers. Nothing in the text says what distinguishes the 1,401 teacher-years and 580 teachers with a missing index, or whether they differ systematically. This propagates into Table 7: the two- and three-group tournament columns are estimated on N = 30,479 even though teachers are, by the text's own description, 'divided into two ... or three ... groups based on the classroom quality index' — the grouping variable is missing for 1,401 of those observations, and how they were assigned is not stated.
- The reported number of unique teachers in the survey sample is internally inconsistent. The text and Table 1 state 10,991 survey observations from 3,345 unique teachers (3.32 years per teacher), but Table 2 columns 7–12, Table 3 Panel B, and Table 5 Panel B all report 'N (teachers)' of 4,066 (4,067 in column 12) for the same 10,990–10,991 observations, implying 2.70 years per teacher. In the observation columns the identically labeled row does match the unique-teacher counts (10,934 and 10,354), so the same label is carrying two different meanings, and one of the two survey figures is unexplained. The effective number of clusters / fixed-effect groups is not something a reader can pin down for the survey results.
- The classroom quality index — the paper's central regressor — cannot be reproduced exactly. The text says it is the first principal component of student-level standardized test scores, GPA, attendance, suspensions and grade repetition, aggregated to the classroom. It does not say whether the PCA is run on the correlation or covariance matrix, whether it is estimated pooled across all years or separately by year or grade, how students missing one or more components are handled (listwise deletion versus imputation), whether the student-level index is standardized before classroom averaging, or the sign convention. The component loadings exist only in Supplemental Appendix Table A4.
- The two survey and observation composites are underspecified. For the survey score, note 2 says items originally on a 1–5 scale 'are mapped to 1–4' without giving the mapping rule (linear rescaling? category collapse? which categories?), says three items are reverse-coded without identifying which three, and says missing values 'are ignored' with no minimum-item or minimum-respondent-per-teacher threshold; the 36 items and their assignment to the seven indices are only in Appendix Table A3. For the observation score, the text describes 19 rubric components rated on a four-point scale that are 'aggregated into a single teacher practice score,' and then defines the outcome as the 'final score averaged across four domains,' without stating how components map into domain scores (equal weights? CPS's own weights?) or reconciling this with REACH's official 100–400 composite described earlier in the same section.
- Both mechanism outcomes are district-produced black boxes. The NWEA-based value-added measures and the district-developed performance-task summative scores serve as the dependent variables in Table 6 — the paper's principal evidence that classroom quality does not raise objective productivity, and therefore that evaluator bias rather than genuine practice change drives the results — yet the article explicitly declines to describe their construction ('There is already an extensive body of literature on the construction and use of VAMs, which is not the focus of this article'). A replicator cannot regenerate either measure; they can only take CPS's delivered values.
- Much of the robustness architecture is invisible to a reader of the article itself. Thirteen supplemental exhibits are cited (Tables A1–A14 and Figure A1), and seven of them carry load-bearing checks: A6 (later principal components), A7 (full vector of achievement and behavior in place of the index), A9 (observation results re-estimated on the survey sample, which supplies the 0.13 SD comparison figure), A11 (correlated-shocks test underpinning Assumption 1), A12 (between- versus within-school sorting, which motivates the entire policy design), A13 (survey policy simulation), and A14 (turnover). None is reproduced in the article, so the reader who has only the published PDF must accept the paper's characterization of them on trust.
- The policy simulation, which generates the headline equity claim, is not specified tightly enough to reproduce. It is not stated whether the three-group tournament uses terciles or some other cutpoints, whether grouping is done within year, within school, within grade, or pooled, or over what population percentile ranks are computed (within year? pooled across all teacher-years?). The reported magnitudes — Black teachers gaining 7.2 percentile points under the two-group tournament, 8.9 under the three-group, and 8.3 under the regression adjustment — are sensitive to those unstated choices.
- Uncertainty reporting is thin by contemporary standards: standard errors and significance stars only, with no confidence intervals and no exact p-values anywhere in the article. No multiple-comparison adjustment is applied across the 14 placebo estimates in Table 5, the four observation domains in A8, the seven survey domains in A10, or the six subgroup splits in Table 3, though the authors do note in passing that the isolated t+1 estimate should be read cautiously given the number of tests. There is no pre-registration or pre-analysis plan — unsurprising for retrospective administrative work, but relevant given how many subgroup and specification cuts are reported.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Treat the headline estimates (0.068 SD on observation scores, 0.152 SD on survey scores per 1 SD of the classroom quality index) as reproducible in principle but not independently verified: nothing in the published article permits any check without the CPS files. The realistic replication path is a data-sharing agreement with the UChicago Consortium on School Research — where the lead author is a senior research analyst and the second author is an affiliated researcher — plus CPS Research Review Board approval. Because no package is deposited, request the analysis code and the constructed classroom quality index directly from the authors as a first step, not as a fallback.
- Before attempting any replication, request four specific pieces of documentation: (a) the PCA specification — correlation versus covariance matrix, estimation sample (pooled versus by year or grade), missing-component handling, sign convention, and whether the student index is standardized before classroom aggregation — together with the Appendix A4 loadings; (b) the 1–5 to 1–4 survey mapping rule, the identity of the three reverse-coded items, and any minimum-items or minimum-respondents threshold; (c) the aggregation from 19 rubric components to four domain scores to the reported average, and how that relates to REACH's official 100–400 composite; (d) the roster-construction and drop sequence with the starting teacher-year count.
- Obtain the Supplemental Appendix before relying on the robustness narrative. Tables A9, A11, A12, A6 and A7 carry most of the weight behind the two core interpretive claims — that baseline achievement and behavior rather than demographics drive the effect, and that within-teacher composition shocks are as good as random — and A12 is the exhibit that justifies the policy simulations. A reader working from the article PDF alone is accepting all of that on the authors' summary characterization.
- Ask the authors what defines the 1,401 teacher-year observations (580 teachers) with a missing classroom quality index, whether they differ systematically from the estimation sample, and specifically how the Table 7 tournament columns are estimated on N = 30,479 when the grouping variable is missing for those observations. If the missing-index cases are concentrated in small or unusual rosters, the index-based results and the demographics-only column (Table 2, column 6) are not estimated on the same population, which weakens the paper's index-versus-demographics contrast.
- Ask which teacher count is correct for the survey sample — 3,345 (text and Table 1) or 4,066 (Table 2, 3 and 5 'N (teachers)') — and, if the larger figure counts teacher-by-school cells rather than teachers, why the observation columns report unique teachers under the same label. Since the survey specifications with fixed effects use robust rather than clustered standard errors, knowing the true number of teachers and of fixed-effect groups matters for how much to discount the survey-sample precision.
- Confirm the panel years before computing anything from the reported Ns: the text says 2012–2013 through 2016–2017, the Table 1 note says 2011–2012 through 2016–2017, and REACH applied only to non-tenured teachers in 2012–2013. If the first year is included, the year-specific standardization is computed on a differently composed population in that year, which affects the interpretation of every standardized coefficient.
- Do not treat Table 6 as an independently checkable test. The negative effects of classroom quality on value-added (−0.148 SD) and on performance-task scores (−1.037) constitute the paper's main evidence for evaluator bias over genuine practice change, yet both dependent variables are district-produced measures whose construction is explicitly outside the article's scope. A replicator must accept CPS's value-added and performance-task scoring as given and cannot test whether the negative signs reflect how those measures net out prior achievement — a mechanical possibility the authors themselves raise ('students with higher baseline achievement have less room to grow') but do not rule out.
- Use the available public sources for partial external triangulation of context rather than of estimates: CPS and Consortium reports on REACH (Sartain et al., 2020; Sporte & Jiang, 2016; CPS, 2019) document the evaluation system's rubric, weighting, and rating distributions, and school-level 5Essentials results are publicly posted. These can corroborate the institutional description and the descriptive pattern in Figure 1, but nothing public can verify any within-teacher estimate in the paper.
- Read the null and borderline results with the reporting limits in mind. With stars and standard errors but no confidence intervals or exact p-values, several consequential claims — the null placebo estimates in Table 5, the significant t+1 coefficient (0.033, SE 0.016), the marginal prior-observation-score interaction (0.032, SE 0.018), and the non-significant Hispanic (0.038, SE 0.028) and Black-teacher survey (0.059, SE 0.067) heterogeneity estimates — should be converted to implied intervals from the reported SEs before being read as evidence of no effect. Several of those intervals comfortably contain the full-sample point estimate, so 'no significant difference across groups' is a statement about precision as much as about homogeneity.
- If you are considering acting on the policy simulation (the ~8 percentile-point gain for Black teachers), request the exact ranking and grouping algorithm — cutpoints for the three-group tournament, and the unit within which groups and percentile ranks are formed (year, school, grade, or pooled). The equity magnitude is the paper's most quotable result and is the least reproducible from the published description.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This is a well-documented empirical paper with essentially no open-science apparatus, and the two halves should be judged separately. On specification transparency it is genuinely strong: Equation 4's right-hand side is enumerated in prose down to the omitted racial category and the two 'missing credential' indicators; the fixed-effect structure (teacher-by-school plus year) is stated; the standard-error rule is stated and consistently applied across table notes; standardization conventions are restated in every note; and each column reports N, N (teachers), R-squared, and control-set indicators. Someone holding the CPS extract could sit down with the article and write the main regression without contacting the authors. The garbled equations in the text extraction used for this review are a PDF-conversion artifact, not a defect of the article; the prose surrounding each equation carries enough content to reconstruct Equations 1–2 and 4–7 regardless.

Where it falls short is in everything upstream of the regression. Three of the paper's key variables are constructed objects whose recipes are incomplete. The classroom quality index is the paper's central regressor and appears in every headline number, yet the PCA is described in one sentence with the loadings relegated to an appendix table not bound with the article; a replicator must guess at the matrix type, the estimation sample, the missing-data rule, and the standardization order, and small choices there shift the index and hence every coefficient scaled in its standard deviations. The survey composite has a stated but unspecified 1–5 to 1–4 mapping, three unnamed reverse-coded items, and a missing-data rule ('ignored') with no minimum-response floor. The observation composite is described as an average across four domains without the component-to-domain aggregation rule and without reconciliation to the REACH 100–400 composite the same section describes. None of this makes the paper wrong; it makes the numbers non-reconstructible to more than a rough approximation.

Three numerical inconsistencies are worth flagging because a replicator will hit them immediately and cannot resolve them from the text. First, the 1,401-observation, 580-teacher gap between the full sample (30,479) and the classroom-quality-index sample (29,078) is visible in Table 1 and structures Table 2, but is never described — and it becomes substantive in Table 7, where the tournament policy columns report N = 30,479 despite grouping teachers on a variable missing for 1,401 of them. Second, the survey sample's unique-teacher count is 3,345 in the text and Table 1 but 4,066 in the 'N (teachers)' row of Tables 2, 3 and 5, while the same row in the observation columns does track unique teachers. Third, the panel is described as 2012–13 through 2016–17 in the text and 2011–12 through 2016–17 in the Table 1 note, with the added wrinkle that REACH covered only non-tenured teachers in the first of those years. Each is small on its own; together they mean a replicator cannot confirm they have assembled the same dataset.

On data access, the paper does better than a bare citation and worse than current journal norms. The sources, provider, and institutional relationships are named with enough specificity that the access route is inferable — de-identified CPS administrative and REACH files plus 5Essentials survey data through the UChicago Consortium on School Research, with the Consortium and the CPS Talent Office thanked by name, and the lead author employed by the Consortium. But there is no data availability statement, no described application procedure, no research-review-board reference, and no code of any kind. Nothing in the article, including the Funding, Conflicts, and ORCID back matter, addresses reproducibility. Restricted administrative data are a legitimate reason not to post data; they are not a reason not to post code, describe an access pathway, or name the software used. The absence of all three is the main reason this review does not sit higher.

The practical consequence for readers: the descriptive facts (Figure 1's raw gradient, Table 1's sample composition) and the specification logic are checkable on their face, while the causal estimates, every robustness check, and the policy simulation are effectively unverifiable without a CPS data agreement — and several of them are unverifiable even by a reader with the data, because the appendix carrying the checks does not travel with the article. The mechanism claim in Table 6, which is what elevates the paper from 'ratings correlate with composition' to 'this is evaluator bias,' rests entirely on two district-produced measures the authors explicitly decline to describe; that claim should be treated as the least independently checkable in the paper. Rating 'adequate' rather than 'weak' reflects that the central specification and its samples are reported clearly enough to understand and, given data, re-run; rating it no higher reflects that a 2026 article in an AERA journal offers the reader no data statement, no code, no software environment, and no route to the supplement's load-bearing exhibits.
